Objective Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease characterized by initial involvement of the olfactory bulb/amygdala or autonomic nerves followed by nigral degeneration. Although autonomic innervation strictly regulates multiorgan systems, including endocrine functions, circulation, and digestion, how dysautonomia in PD affects systemic metabolism has not been identified. In this study, we tried to estimate the pathogenic linkage of PD by nuclear medicine techniques, trans‐omic analysis of blood samples, and cultured cell experiments. Methods Thyroid mediastinum ratio of 123 I‐metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy was measured in 1,158 patients with PD. Furthermore, serum exosome miRNA transcriptome analysis and plasma metabolome analysis followed by trans‐omic analysis were performed in patients with de novo PD and age‐matched healthy control persons. Additionally, thyroid hormone was administered to skeletal muscle and liver derived cells to evaluate the effect of hypothyroidism for these organs. Results Sympathetic denervation of thyroid correlating with its cardiac denervation was confirmed in 1,158 patients with PD by MIBG scintigraphy. Among patients with drug‐naïve PD, comprehensive metabolome analysis revealed decreased levels of thyroxine and insufficient fatty acid β‐oxidation, which positively correlate with one another. Likewise, both plasma metabolome data and transcriptome data of circulating exosomal miRNAs, revealed specific enrichment of the peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor (PPARα) axis. Finally, association of thyroid hormone with PPARα‐dependent β‐oxidation regulation was confirmed by in vitro experiments. Interpretation Our findings suggest that interorgan communications between the thyroid and liver are disorganized in the early stage of PD, which would be a sensitive diagnostic biomarker for PD. Hormones, cytokines, growth factors, and immunoglobulins connect isolated organs throughout the body to regulate whole‐body metabolism. 9 Although metabolic changes in amino acids, kynurenine, caffeine, fatty acids (FAs), and polyamines in the serum/plasma of patients with PD have been identified by us and others, those arising from dysautonomia remain unclear. 10 , 11 , 12 The thyroid is one of the most important organs regulating metabolism of the brain, white fat, brown fat, skeletal muscles, and liver, mainly under control of the hypothalamus‐pituitary‐thyroid axis. 13 In addition, use of animal models has delineated a functional role for sympathetic innervation on thyroid hormone secretion. 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 In humans, blood supplied from the intrathyroidal artery is regulated by sympathetic nerves, mainly from the cervical ganglia along the artery. 13 Sympathetic innervation of the thyroid in healthy humans was confirmed by 6‐ 18 F‐fluorodopamine imaging with/without desipramine, an inhibitor of serotonin/noradrenaline uptake. 18 In patients with PD, significant decreases of MIBG or 6‐ 18 F‐fluorodopamine uptake in the thyroid have been identified. 18 , 19 , 20 Horsager et al found that postganglionic autonomic denervation is initiated from celiac or mesenteric ganglions and retrogradely expanded to cervical ganglia in one subtype of PD. 21 Because pharmacologic doses of dopamine, glucocorticoids, and somatostatin suppress thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), 22 it remains unclear how thyroid function affects downstream target organs, such as skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and liver in PD treated with/without L‐DOPA and/or dopamine agonists. Here, we report sympathetic denervation of the thyroid by cardiac MIBG scintigraphy in patients with PD, especially those with constipation, that correlated with cardiac denervation and nigral dopamine degeneration. Moreover, we identified suppression of FA β‐oxidation and its positive correlation with thyroxine levels in patients with de novo PD. To investigate interorgan communication, we performed transcriptome analysis of circulating serum exosomal miRNAs, which may serve as mediators among organs and appropriate diagnostic biomarkers for several diseases compared with non‐exosomal miRNAs. 23 , 24 , 25 Based on these assays, the peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor (PPARα) axis was enriched. Finally, we confirmed an association between thyroid hormone and the PPARα pathway in the liver using cultured human cell lines, proposing inter‐tissue communication in early PD.

core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Confirmed in 1,158 PD patients with decreased early/delayed H/M ratios and SBR of DaT-SPECT. Early T/M ratio (thyroidal denervation) was significantly decreased in PD, and significantly lower in early PD with constipation. Thyroidal denervation correlated with cardiac denervation and nigral dopamine degeneration.

Insufficient in drug-naïve PD, positively correlates with thyroxine levels. Suppressed in de novo PD without medication. Reconfirmed in early-stage PD (H&Y I-II).

Specific enrichment identified by plasma metabolome and circulating exosomal miRNA transcriptome data. Pathway significantly altered, contributing to metabolomic and transcriptomic changes. In vitro, PPARα knockdown suppressed CPT1A mRNA and protein levels.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: de novo Parkinson's disease (PD) exosomal transcriptome
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: 141 significantly changed miRNAs identified, with 101 being upregulated. Upregulated miRNAs indicate alterations in FA biosynthesis and thyroid signaling.

63 significantly changed metabolites identified. Decreased levels of 12 long-chain acylcarnitines (LC-ACs) and increased levels of 11 long-chain fatty acids (LC-FAs) were observed, with significant correlations to thyroxine.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: de novo Parkinson's disease (PD) without medication

core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in early PD patients with OH compared to those without OH. All PD patients with OH had abnormal blood pressure responses to Valsalva maneuver.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Early Parkinson's Disease (PD) pathogenesis, particularly focusing on dysautonomia and thyroid-liver axis metabolic regulation.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Sympathetic denervation of the thyroid, correlating with cardiac denervation and nigral dopamine degeneration, leads to disorganized interorgan communication between the thyroid and liver in early PD. This disruption results in decreased thyroxine levels, which consequently impacts the liver's metabolic functions, specifically peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα)-dependent fatty acid β-oxidation. Exosomal miRNAs are proposed as key messengers in this inter-tissue communication, regulating gene expression in pathways like 'Fatty acid biosynthesis', 'Thyroid hormone signaling pathway', and 'Fatty acid metabolism'. The thyroid hormone, primarily T3, regulates PPARα-mediated CPT1A expression, which is crucial for fatty acid β-oxidation mainly in the liver. This systemic neurodegeneration, observed as thyroidal sympathetic denervation, follows a caudo-rostral pattern, especially in early PD patients with constipation. Decreasing thyroid hormone and PPARα signaling may induce systemic insults contributing to neurodegeneration.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Thyroid hormone (T3) increased CPT1A gene expression in HepG2 cells in an almost dose-dependent manner. Comparisons between 'early PD with constipation' and 'early PD without constipation' revealed distinct findings; early T/M ratio (thyroidal denervation) was significantly lower only in PD patients with constipation, whereas early H/M ratios (cardiac denervation) were significantly decreased in both groups. T3 upregulated mitochondrial respiration via PGC1α in hepatic cell lines, but did not upregulate β-oxidation in primary skeletal muscle cell lines, demonstrating tissue-specific effects. A significantly higher prevalence of Orthostatic Hypotension was observed in early PD with OH compared to early PD without OH, differentiating these patient groups.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The observed metabolic alterations and denervation were specific to Parkinson's Disease (PD) when compared to non-PD groups (healthy controls, drug-induced parkinsonism, essential tremor). Specifically, early and delayed H/M ratios and SBR of DaT-SPECT were significantly decreased in PD patients. The early T/M ratio was found to be significantly lower in patients with early PD and constipation, but not in those without constipation, suggesting it as a specific marker for a subtype of early PD with systemic autonomic dysfunction. T3's effect on CPT1A (liver isoform) but not CPT1B (skeletal muscle isoform) highlights tissue specificity. MIBG uptake in the thyroid primarily reflects sympathetic neuronal activity, as thyroidal blockade did not alter T/M ratios. Fatty acid β-oxidation insufficiency was specifically detected in patients with early-stage PD (H&Y I-II) and de novo PD.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients with early, de novo, and drug-naïve Parkinson's disease (PD), including specific subtypes presenting with constipation or orthostatic hypotension. Study included age-matched healthy controls, patients with drug-induced parkinsonism, essential tremor, and utilized human hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) and primary human skeletal myotubular cell lines.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The study uncovers systemic metabolic alterations in early PD, driven by disorganized interorgan communication between the thyroid and liver due to sympathetic denervation. This leads to decreased thyroxine levels and insufficient fatty acid β-oxidation, which may induce systemic insults to both the body and brain, potentially contributing to neurodegeneration. The findings highlight the role of altered exosomal miRNAs and the PPARα pathway in these metabolic dysregulations and their contribution to PD pathogenesis. Decreased MIBG uptake by the thyroid and modestly decreased serum thyroid hormones are observed in early/de novo PD, reflecting a systemic neurodegeneration pattern.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility: The findings suggest that thyroidal sympathetic denervation (e.g., early T/M ratio), in conjunction with cardiac denervation and dopaminergic degeneration, holds potential as a sensitive diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for early-stage PD, especially for subtypes with pronounced autonomic dysfunction like constipation. Metabolomic and exosomal miRNA profiles also show diagnostic promise. Adverse risk: Suppressed fatty acid β-oxidation and hypothyroidism in de novo PD indicate significant metabolic dysfunction contributing to the disease pathology and potential systemic insults.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of key biomarkers is supported by their consistency with previous reports and established criteria, as well as significant statistical correlations (e.g., early H/M and T/M ratios correlated with disease severity and serum thyroxine levels). Exosomal miRNAs are considered highly reliable diagnostic messengers due to their resistance to degradation in the bloodstream and their ability to reflect the state of parental cells. MIBG uptake in the thyroid reliably reflects sympathetic neuronal activity, validated by experiments with thyroidal blockade.
recommended_alternatives: Serum exosomal miRNAs (recommended over non-exosomal miRNAs for diagnostic and pathophysiological studies)
Further research is required to resolve issues concerning the pathogenic sequence of neurodegeneration in PD and the specific pathological role of α-Syn deposition.
The involvement of the parasympathetic nervous system, including the vagal nerve, should be considered for further analysis using 11C-donepezil positron emission tomography-computed tomography.
